A bat mitzvah is a Jewish coming-of-age milestone for girls. The phrase comes from Hebrew and Aramaic and means "daughter of the commandment." In Jewish religious law, a "commandment" (called a mitzvah, plural: mitzvot) is a divine obligation — a rule or duty that Jewish people are expected to follow as part of their faith.

When a Jewish girl reaches a certain age (traditionally 12 years old, though many modern communities use 13), she is considered to have crossed a threshold: she is now spiritually and religiously an adult. From this moment on, she is personally responsible for observing all the mitzvot — the religious duties — that Jewish law places on her. Before this point, that responsibility belonged to her parents. After it, it belongs to her.

So in its most literal, technical sense, a bat mitzvah is the girl herself — she is a "daughter of the commandment," meaning she has become a full moral and religious agent within Judaism. You don't just have a bat mitzvah; strictly speaking, you become one. The phrase describes her new status, not merely an event she attends.

That said, in common usage, the word "bat mitzvah" has also come to refer to the ceremony and celebration that marks this transition — which is how most people use it today.

To understand why this matters so much, you need to understand a little about how Judaism views religious obligation.

In Jewish law, every Jewish person above a certain age is bound by a set of commandments — rules about prayer, food, observance of holy days, ethical behavior, and much more. A child is not yet fully bound by these. But once a girl turns 12 (or a boy turns 13, as discussed below), she or he is now fully accountable before God for fulfilling these obligations.

This is not just a symbolic gesture. It means the young person can now:

  • Be counted as a full adult member of the Jewish community in religious contexts
  • Be called to read from the Torah (the Jewish holy scripture) publicly during worship
  • Lead certain prayers and religious rituals (in many denominations)
  • Sign religious legal documents
  • Take on the full weight of Jewish religious life independently

The bat mitzvah moment is therefore not just a party. It is a legal and spiritual transformation in the eyes of Jewish religious law.

The bat mitzvah ceremony is typically held at a synagogue (a Jewish house of worship), most often on a Saturday morning, which is the Jewish Sabbath — the holiest day of the week and the most important time for communal worship and Torah reading.

During the ceremony, the bat mitzvah girl (the one being honored) typically:

  • Reads aloud from the Torah scroll — a handwritten parchment scroll containing the Five Books of Moses. The reading is in Hebrew, chanted according to a traditional melodic system. Each week, a specific portion (parasha) of the Torah is read, and the bat mitzvah will read (or chant) from that week's assigned portion.
  • Reads from the Haftarah — a related passage from the Prophets section of the Hebrew Bible, also chanted in Hebrew.
  • Delivers a speech (called a d'var Torah, meaning "word of Torah") — a short talk in which she discusses the meaning or lesson of the Torah portion she read, often connecting it to her own life or values.

This demonstrates that she has studied Hebrew, learned to read sacred texts, and can now participate as a full adult in Jewish worship.

A bat mitzvah is not something a girl simply shows up to. It typically requires years of preparation, including:

  • Attending Hebrew school to learn the Hebrew language and Jewish religious traditions
  • Learning to read from the Torah, which is written without vowels or musical notations and must be chanted correctly from memory or close study
  • Studying her specific Torah portion in depth
  • Working with a rabbi (a Jewish religious leader) or a tutor

This preparation itself is considered a crucial part of the process — it is the education that makes her ready to take on adult religious responsibility.

Following the religious ceremony, it is customary to hold a celebratory gathering — often a party or reception — with family and friends. In many communities, especially in the United States, these celebrations have grown into elaborate, joyful events with food, music, dancing, and gifts.

It is important to note, however, that the party is a cultural tradition layered on top of the ceremony — it is not what makes someone a bat mitzvah. The religious status is conferred by the age and the Jewish community's recognition of it, with or without a ceremony or party. Even a girl who never has any formal ceremony at all still becomes a bat mitzvah at age 12 simply by reaching that age — the ceremony is a public, communal celebration of something that happens regardless.
How it differs from a bar mitzvah

The male equivalent is called a bar mitzvah — "son of the commandment." The age for boys is 13 (not 12 like girls). The structure of the ceremony is essentially the same.

Historically, the bar mitzvah has existed as a formal ceremony for centuries. The bat mitzvah ceremony for girls is much newer — the first recorded formal bat mitzvah ceremony in the modern sense was held in 1922 in New York, for a rabbi's daughter. Before that, girls' coming-of-age was acknowledged quietly or not at all in most Jewish communities, even though the legal status still applied to them.

Today, whether and how a bat mitzvah ceremony is conducted varies significantly across different branches of Judaism:

  • Orthodox Judaism tends to have more limited or separate ceremonies for girls, often not including public Torah reading by women, due to traditional interpretations of religious law.
  • Conservative, Reform, Reconstructionist, and other liberal denominations generally conduct bat mitzvah ceremonies that are nearly identical in scope and format to bar mitzvah ceremonies.

When referring to multiple people or events, the word takes a Hebrew plural form. Multiple girls who have become bat mitzvah are called b'not mitzvah (daughters of the commandment). Together, boys and girls who have come of age are called b'nei mitzvah (children of the commandment). In casual English, people often just say "bat mitzvahs" when referring to multiple ceremonies.

A bat mitzvah is, at once, a person (a Jewish girl who has crossed the threshold into religious adulthood at age 12), a legal and spiritual status (the responsibility for fulfilling the Jewish commandments now rests on her, not her parents), and a ceremony (a public, communal celebration — usually at a synagogue on Saturday — where she reads from the Torah and is recognized as a full adult member of the Jewish faith). It represents one of the most meaningful milestones in a Jewish girl's life, marking the moment she steps fully into the religious tradition she was raised in and takes ownership of it for herself.
1546:
A batch is a group of things of the same kind that are made, collected, or handled together, at one time.

The key thought behind this word is: instead of doing things one by one, you do them as a group, all at once. That group is a batch.

Three things are always true about a batch:

1. The items are similar or of the same type.
You make a batch of cookies — not a batch of cookies and a random chair thrown in. The things in a batch belong together because they're the same kind of thing.

2. They are grouped together deliberately.
A batch isn't a random pile. Someone consciously decides: "These things go together." They are collected or produced as one defined set.

3. They are made or dealt with together, in one go.
This is the heart of the word. The items in a batch share the same "session" — the same baking session, the same production run, the same processing moment.

Imagine a baker. She puts 12 cookies in the oven at 9 AM. Those 12 cookies come out together. That is one batch. Then at 10 AM, she puts another 12 cookies in. That is a second batch.

Notice: she didn't bake 24 cookies all at once. She baked them in batches — one group at a time. This is the most natural, intuitive example of the word.

The word travels across many areas of life, always carrying the same core meaning:

In cooking and baking:
"I made three batches of muffins for the party." Each time you bake a set of muffins, that's one batch.

In manufacturing and production:
Factories make products in batches. A pharmaceutical company might manufacture 10,000 bottles of medicine together in one production run — that is one batch. If something goes wrong, they can trace exactly which batch was affected (this is why medicine bottles have a "batch number" on them).

In computing:
A "batch" of data or tasks means a set of items that are processed together by a computer in one operation, rather than one at a time or in real time. For example, a bank might process all of the day's transactions at midnight in one batch, rather than updating your account every single second.

In everyday life:
The word is used loosely and naturally for any group of similar things that arrive or are dealt with together:

  • "A batch of emails" — a bunch of emails that came in together.
  • "A batch of new students" — a group of students who joined the school at the same time.
  • "A batch of applications" — a set of job applications received in the same period.
  • "A fresh batch of problems" — a new set of issues to solve.
A Subtle But Important Quality: Batches Imply Repetition

When someone says "a batch," they naturally suggest that there are, or could be, other batches. It's not just one single, unique group — it's one of potentially many rounds.

This is different from saying "a group" or "a collection," which don't carry that sense of repetition. "A batch" tells you: this is one round of something that happens in rounds.

A batch can be tiny or enormous. A batch of two cookies is still a batch. A batch of a million car parts is still a batch. What matters is not how big the group is, but the fact that the items were made or handled together, as one defined set.

• "a fresh batch" — a newly made or newly arrived group. "There's a fresh batch of bread at the bakery."
  • "in batches" — doing something group by group rather than all at once. "We'll process the orders in batches."
  • "a batch of" — the standard way to use the word, followed by whatever the items are. "A batch of reports."
  • "batch number" — an identification number assigned to a particular batch during production, used for tracking.
  • "the first/second/next batch" — specifying which round or group you mean.
A batch is a defined group of similar things that are produced, processed, or handled together, in one session — one of potentially many such rounds.
1547: "Bate" is a word with several distinct meanings, depending on the context in which it is used. Each meaning belongs to a different world — one to everyday language, one to the world of birds, one to leathermaking, and one to British slang.
Meaning 1: To Hold Back, Reduce, or Restrain Something

This is the core and most important meaning of "bate." When you bate something, you hold it back, tone it down, or reduce its strength or intensity. You are keeping something from going at full force.

Think of it like turning down a dial — not switching something off, but making it quieter, weaker, or less intense.

Examples:

  • A nervous student waiting outside the exam hall waits with bated breath — meaning they are holding their breath, almost afraid to breathe, out of suspense or excitement. Their breathing is restrained, pulled back.
  • A judge might bate the strictness of a punishment — meaning they soften it, reduce it.
  • "He could not bate his excitement as the results were announced." — He could not hold his excitement back.

"With bated breath" is by far the most common place you will encounter this meaning of the word. If you've ever read or heard someone say "everyone waited with bated breath," now you know exactly what it means: with breath held back, tightly restrained — the physical thing a person does when they are tense, anxious, or deeply eager.
Meaning 2: To Beat the Wings Wildly (Falconry)

In the world of falconry — the ancient practice of training birds of prey like hawks and falcons to hunt — "bate" has a very specific meaning.

When a hawk bates, it beats its wings frantically and tries to fly off the falconer's gloved fist or its perch, but it is held back by its jesses (the leather straps attached to its legs). The bird panics, flutters violently, and hangs mid-air for a moment before being settled back down.

A hawk might bate out of fear, excitement, or agitation. It is an involuntary, impulsive reaction — the bird cannot control itself. A well-trained hawk bates less and less over time.

Example:

  • "The young falcon bated every time a stranger came near." — It flapped and lurched off the perch in fear.
Meaning 3: To Soak and Soften Hides (Leathermaking / Tanning)

In the craft of tanning — turning raw animal hides into leather — "bate" refers to a specific step in the process.

After the hair is removed from a hide, the skin is still stiff and harsh. To soften it and make it workable, tanners bate the hide by soaking it in a special alkaline liquid or solution containing enzymes. This breaks down unwanted proteins and relaxes the fibres of the skin, making it soft, supple, and ready for the next step of tanning.

So when you bate a hide, you are essentially treating it with a softening bath.

Example:

  • "The skins were bated overnight in a warm solution before tanning could begin."
Meaning 4: To Be in a Rage (British Informal)

In informal British English — particularly in older usage and in certain regional dialects — if someone is bating, they are in a furious temper. "A bate" (used as a noun here too) means a fit of rage or a bad mood.

Examples:

  • "Don't bate at me — it wasn't my fault!" — Don't rage at me.
  • "He came home in a right bate." — He came home absolutely furious. (noun form, but worth knowing alongside the verb)

This meaning is not used widely in modern, formal, or international English, but you may come across it in British literature or conversation.

This is an old and now largely obsolete meaning. In earlier English, to bate something from a sum meant to take it away or deduct it.

Example:

  • "Bate a few pence from the price, and we have a deal." — Subtract a few pence.

You are unlikely to encounter this meaning in modern writing except in very old texts or historical novels.
A Quick Summary of All the Meanings

• Restrain / reduce / hold back → "with bated breath" (most common and important)
  • A hawk fluttering wildly off a perch → falconry term
  • Soften a hide in tanning solution → leathermaking
  • Be in a furious rage → British informal
  • Deduct or subtract → archaic, rarely used today
The One You Must Know Cold

Of all these meanings, "bate" meaning to hold back or restrain is the one that matters most to you as a learner, because it lives on in the phrase "with bated breath" — which is extremely common in literature, journalism, and everyday speech. Now that you know what "bate" truly means, that phrase will never be a mystery to you again. You will read it and instantly understand: someone is holding back even their very breath — so tense, so eager, so gripped by anticipation that they can barely breathe.
1548:
Bathetic describes something that creates a jarring, deflating feeling — either because it suddenly drops from something grand and serious down to something trivial and silly, or because it is dripping with so much forced, fake emotion that it feels cheap and manipulative rather than genuinely moving.

It is the adjective form of the noun bathos. Think of bathos as the opposite of the feeling you get when something lives up to its dramatic buildup. Bathos is what happens when that buildup collapses — either into absurdity, or into hollow tearjerking.

There are two flavors of bathetic, and both matter.

This is the most classic use. Something is bathetic when it starts at a high, serious, or grand level — and then crashes down without warning into something embarrassingly small or mundane.

Think of it this way: imagine someone building a magnificent cathedral, brick by brick, floor by floor, reaching the sky — and then placing a plastic garden gnome on top as the final touch. That gnome is bathetic. It doesn't belong. It kills the grandeur instantly.

Example in writing:

"He had survived two world wars, escaped from a prisoner-of-war camp, and crossed three continents on foot. Last Thursday, he slipped on a banana peel."

The last sentence is bathetic. The list builds and builds — war, escape, heroism — and then collapses into slapstick. The crash is so sudden and so steep that it is almost funny. That collision between the grand and the ridiculous is exactly what bathetic means in this sense.

This is why bathetic writing often has an unintentionally comic effect, even when the writer intended to be serious. If you write a solemn, heartbreaking eulogy and accidentally end it with a trivial sentence, the result is bathetic — and the audience might laugh or cringe at exactly the wrong moment.

Another example:

"The storm was apocalyptic. Lightning split the sky. Thunder shook the earth. She worried she might get her hair wet."

The last line is bathetic. It yanks you from the dramatic storm down to a petty vanity, and the tonal collision is jarring.
Flavor 2: Fake or Overdone Emotion (False Sentimentality)

The second meaning is slightly different. Here, something is bathetic not because of an abrupt tonal drop, but because it is wallowing in emotion so heavily and so artificially that it stops feeling real and starts feeling manipulative or embarrassing.

Think of a TV commercial that uses slow piano music, a child with wide tearful eyes, and soft golden lighting — all to sell you a brand of paper towels. The emotion is performed, not earned. It is designed to squeeze a feeling out of you through sheer manipulation, not through anything genuinely moving. That is bathetic.

Or think of a soap opera scene where a character weeps dramatically and delivers a ten-minute monologue about a problem that most people would handle with a phone call. The emotion is so exaggerated, so much more than the situation warrants, that it tips over into something cringeworthy. That is also bathetic.

In this sense, bathetic overlaps with words like maudlin (weepily sentimental) or saccharine (sickeningly sweet), but bathetic carries the specific idea that the emotion fails — it tries to move you but instead makes you roll your eyes, or feel vaguely manipulated.

A useful way to think about it: Genuine pathos (real, earned emotion) makes you feel. Bathetic emotion makes you aware that you are being made to feel — and that awareness kills the effect. The curtain gets pulled back, and you see the machinery.

This is an important distinction that many people miss.

Unintentional bathos is a writing flaw. The writer wanted to be solemn, grand, or deeply moving — but the result is deflating or hollow. This is the kind that makes readers cringe or snicker at a funeral scene.

Intentional bathos is a literary device — and a powerful one. Writers, comedians, and poets use it deliberately to create comic effect, to deflate pomposity, or to mock something by treating it with absurdly mismatched grandeur. Alexander Pope, one of history's most celebrated poets, built an entire famous poem (The Rape of the Lock) on intentional bathos — he used the full, epic, heroic style of ancient war poetry to describe a petty social squabble over a stolen lock of hair. The joke works because the mismatch between style and subject is so bathetic.

So when you call something bathetic, context tells you whether it is a failure or a carefully aimed joke.

Because the two words sound so similar, people confuse them constantly — but they mean completely different things.

Pathetic (from pathos) means either arousing pity and sadness, or — in everyday informal use — pitifully inadequate ("that excuse is pathetic").

Bathetic (from bathos) means characterized by an anticlimactic crash from the grand to the trivial, or by false/overdone sentimentality.

The connection between them is that bathos is essentially what happens when an attempt at genuine pathos goes wrong — when emotion is so overdone or so poorly placed that it collapses. But the two words are not interchangeable.

A person crying at a funeral is pathetic (in the classical, sympathetic sense). A funeral speech that starts with profound words about life and death and ends with a joke about the deceased's bad parking habits is bathetic. A movie that makes you cry is pathetic (in the best sense). A movie that tries too hard to make you cry by piling on obvious emotional triggers until you feel manipulated is bathetic.

You would call something bathetic when:

  • A piece of writing, speech, or performance drops abruptly from a high tone to a trivial one in a way that is deflating or unintentionally comic.
  • A story, film, advertisement, or performance lays emotion on so thick and so artificially that it feels hollow, cloying, or manipulative rather than genuinely touching.

Example sentences:

  • "The speech was supposed to be moving, but the bathetic ending — a joke about his cat — left the audience confused."
  • "The film's final act was so bathetic, so relentlessly tearful and manipulative, that I felt annoyed rather than sad."
  • "It is a bathetic image: a warrior in full armour, weeping over a broken biscuit."

If you ever need to remember what bathetic means: it describes the awkward, deflating, or manipulative failure that happens when something reaches for grandeur or genuine feeling — and instead lands with a thud.
1549:
Bathos is the jarring, often humorous effect created when something grand, serious, or emotionally weighty is suddenly undercut by something trivial, silly, or absurdly mundane. Think of it as a steep drop in dignity — you're climbing a staircase of importance and gravitas, and then, without warning, you fall face-first into a puddle.

The word has two closely related meanings, and understanding both is essential.
The first meaning: an abrupt plunge from the grand to the trivial

This is the most common meaning. It happens when writing, speech, or film builds up something solemn and important — and then immediately deflates it with something petty or absurd. The gap between the two levels is where bathos lives.

Here's a clear example: "She had survived heartbreak, poverty, and the collapse of an entire empire — and then she lost her keys."

Notice how the sentence opens with enormous weight — heartbreak, poverty, the fall of empires — and then suddenly lands on losing keys. That drop, from the colossal to the petty, is bathos. The reader expects the sentence to end somewhere worthy of what came before, and instead it falls off a cliff into the ordinary.

Now, this kind of bathos can be either intentional or unintentional, and the difference matters enormously.

Intentional bathos is a deliberate technique. Skilled writers use it as a tool for comedy, satire, or to gently puncture something that's being too pompous or overblown. When done well, it's genuinely funny — the drop is the joke. Alexander Pope, the 18th-century poet, was a master of this. In The Rape of the Lock, he wrote about a woman having a lock of her hair stolen as though it were an earth-shattering, epic-scale tragedy — full of grand, heroic language — and the entire joke rests on the absurd contrast between the weightiness of the writing and the triviality of the event. He was skewering vanity by using bathos as a scalpel.

Unintentional bathos is the opposite: a writer tries sincerely to be moving or majestic, but accidentally slips into the ridiculous. This is a flaw, not a technique. Imagine a poem that builds toward a devastating emotional peak and then concludes: "O Death, thou conqueror of all — / The brave, the noble, the great, / And Mike from Accounts, who tripped on a ball." The writer probably meant for that last line to feel humanizing and touching. Instead, the casual, mundane detail kills the mood stone dead. The poem tried to be a cathedral and became a garden shed.
The second meaning: excessive, overdone, or fake emotion

The second meaning of bathos is sentimentality taken so far that it collapses into hollowness or even unintentional comedy — emotion that is so exaggerated, so relentlessly laid on, that it stops feeling genuine and starts feeling manipulative or absurd.

Picture a film where every single scene has someone weeping in slow motion, with swelling orchestral music playing underneath, whether the moment earns it or not. After a while, all that heaped-on emotion starts to feel not moving, but exhausting — and eventually laughable. That is bathos. The film was reaching for your heartstrings so desperately and so clumsily that it missed them entirely.

Here, bathos isn't about a sudden drop in tone, but about a collapse under the weight of too much emotion. When you try too hard to make something moving, it stops being moving. It becomes soggy. Genuine pathos (see below) earns its emotion; bathos in this sense begs for it and makes you want to back away.

They share a common thread: in both cases, something fails to achieve the effect it was aiming for — or achieves a deliberately comic version of failure. The first meaning fails by going too low after going high (the sudden drop). The second meaning fails by going too high for too long (the emotional overload). In both cases, the result is a feeling of deflation — either sudden, like a needle popping a balloon, or gradual, like a balloon quietly going flat over days. The key concept in both is a fall from what is elevated.

These two words look nearly identical and are frequently confused, so it's worth being precise. Pathos is genuine, skillfully evoked emotion — the quality in a piece of writing or art that makes you feel something real, because the emotion has been honestly earned. Think of a scene in a novel that makes you cry, not because the writer forced it, but because they built it carefully and truthfully. That's pathos working as it should.

Bathos is what goes wrong: either it's the fake, manufactured version of pathos (the second meaning — overdone emotion that rings hollow), or it's the sudden drop that kills real emotion by introducing something trivial (the first meaning). Pathos elevates; bathos deflates. Pathos trusts the reader; the bathetic kind of excess manipulates them, and the tonal-drop kind blindsides them with the mundane.

These are close relatives but not the same thing. An anticlimax is any disappointing ending or letdown — a story builds and builds, and then fizzles out weakly. Bathos is more specific: it requires that distinct gap in register between the grand and the trivial, and the drop from one to the other. All bathos involves anticlimax, but not all anticlimaxes are bathos. If a thriller novel spends 400 pages building toward a confrontation between hero and villain, and then the villain simply gives up and goes home, that's anticlimactic — flat and disappointing. But if the hero defeats the villain in an epic battle and then immediately trips over his shoelace and falls into a bin, that's bathetic — the gap between the epic and the absurd is right there, and it produces that characteristic drop.

When you want to describe something as exhibiting bathos, the adjective is bathetic. A badly written tragedy might be called bathetic. An overwrought film score might be described as bathetic. An overly dramatic political speech that ends with something embarrassingly small might land bathetically.

Bathos is the effect — comic, cringeworthy, or simply deflating — produced when something solemn or grand is suddenly undercut by the trivial, or when emotion is piled on so excessively that it becomes hollow. It can be deployed on purpose as one of literature's sharpest comic tools, or it can arrive accidentally as a mark of poor craft and misjudgment. Either way, it is always about a fall — from what is high to what is low, from what is genuine to what is overwrought.

Once you know this word, you'll start noticing it everywhere: in clumsy newspaper headlines, in overwrought film scores, in political speeches that reach for greatness and land on a typo — and in the hands of the best satirists who ever lived, who used that fall not as a failure but as a perfectly aimed arrow.
1550: A baton is a short, thin stick or rod — but the word is used in several very different situations, each with its own specific meaning.

This is probably the most widely recognised meaning. When an orchestra or choir performs, the person in charge is called a conductor. The conductor holds a baton — a very thin, lightweight, tapered stick (wider at the grip, tapering to a fine tip) — and waves it in precise patterns to guide the musicians. It helps the musicians know the tempo (speed), rhythm, and dynamics (how loud or soft to play) of the music. The baton essentially extends the conductor's hand, making their gestures more visible to an entire hall full of musicians.

In a relay race — a type of running competition where a team of four runners each run one section of the total distance — the runners must carry and pass a baton. This baton is a short, smooth, hollow cylindrical tube (like a thick pen, but rigid). The first runner carries it, and at the end of their section, they hand it to the next runner. This continues until the final runner crosses the finish line. The rules of the race require that the baton be passed within a designated zone; dropping it or passing it outside that zone can disqualify the team.

A police baton is a solid, heavy stick — usually made of wood, rubber, or hard plastic — carried by police officers and used as a defensive and crowd-control weapon. It is longer and heavier than a conductor's baton, designed to be gripped firmly and used to subdue or push back individuals if necessary. You may have also heard it called a truncheon, nightstick, or billy club — these all refer to the same general object, though the exact design may vary slightly by country or police force.

A drum major is the leader of a marching band — the kind you see performing on a sports field or in a parade. The drum major carries a baton, but this one is quite different from a conductor's baton. It is much larger, heavier, and often decorative, with an ornamental knob or ball at the top. The drum major twirls, throws, and catches this baton as part of a performance while also directing the band. It is both a leadership symbol and a showpiece.

In cooking, batons (sometimes written as "bâtons") refer to vegetables or other foods that have been cut into uniform, stick-shaped pieces — roughly the shape of a thick matchstick or a short finger. For example, a recipe might ask you to cut carrots into batons, meaning you slice them into neat, rectangular sticks of a consistent size. This cut makes cooking more even and also makes the food look neater when plated. Common vegetables cut this way include carrots, celery, courgettes (zucchini), and beetroot.

In heraldry — the formal system of designing and describing coats of arms — a baton is a narrow, diagonal band or strip that crosses the shield. It is similar to another heraldic element called a "bend" but is shorter and does not reach the edges of the shield. Historically, a baton placed on a coat of arms was sometimes used to indicate that a person was born outside of a formal marriage. This is quite a specialised, historical meaning you are unlikely to encounter in everyday life, but it is worth knowing.

Beyond these physical objects, the word baton is commonly used figuratively (as a figure of speech). The phrase "pass the baton" means to transfer a responsibility, role, task, or position of leadership from one person to another. It comes directly from the relay race — just as a runner hands the baton to the next person, a retiring CEO might "pass the baton" to their successor, or a teacher might "pass the baton" to the next generation of students. This phrase is extremely common in everyday English, in news articles, speeches, and conversations.

So, the word baton always refers to some kind of stick or rod, but its exact form and purpose change depending on the context:

  • Music → a slender stick that a conductor uses to lead musicians
  • Athletics → a cylindrical tube passed between relay runners
  • Law enforcement → a heavy stick used by police
  • Marching band → a large, decorative stick twirled by a drum major
  • Cooking → a stick-shaped cut of food
  • Heraldry → a diagonal band on a coat of arms
  • Figuratively → the act of handing over responsibility to someone else

The common thread in all these meanings is the same simple image: a stick, rod, or strip — passed, held, wielded, or displayed as a symbol of direction, authority, or transition.
1551: A battalion is a large unit of soldiers in an army. Think of it as one of the standard "building blocks" that armies are organized into. When a country raises an army, it doesn't just throw all its soldiers into one giant crowd — it organizes them into structured groups of different sizes, and a battalion is one of the most important of those groups.

A battalion typically contains 300 to 800 soldiers, with around 500 being a common rough figure. The exact number depends on the country and the type of army unit (infantry, artillery, engineers, etc.).

A battalion is not just a random collection of soldiers. It is built from smaller units called companies (usually 3 to 5 companies per battalion). Each company is itself made up of even smaller groups called platoons, and platoons are made up of squads.

So the structure from smallest to largest looks like this:

Squad → Platoon → Company → Battalion → Brigade/Regiment → Division → Corps → Army

A battalion sits right in the middle of this chain — large enough to be powerful, small enough to be commanded effectively.

A battalion is typically commanded by a Lieutenant Colonel — a fairly senior officer. This person is often called the battalion commander. Because a battalion has its own command structure, it can often operate somewhat independently on a battlefield, which is why it is considered a fundamental tactical unit in warfare.
Why Is a Battalion Important in Military Terms?

A battalion is considered tactically self-sufficient for many purposes. This means it often has not just its fighting soldiers, but also its own support staff — people handling medical care, logistics, communications, and maintenance. Because of this, a battalion can carry out real military operations on its own, without always needing to rely on larger headquarters above it. This makes it one of the most practical and frequently used units in real-world military operations.
The Word Used Outside the Military (Figurative Meaning)

"Battalion" is also very commonly used in everyday language — not just in military contexts. When people want to describe a large, organized, or imposing group of anything (not just soldiers), they often use this word. The figurative use carries the sense of strength in numbers, organization, and collective force.

Examples:

  • "A battalion of journalists crowded around the president after the speech."
  • "She faced a battalion of problems on her first day at the new job."
  • "The company hired a battalion of lawyers to fight the lawsuit."

In all these cases, the speaker is not talking about actual soldiers. They are using "battalion" to paint a vivid picture of a large number of people (or things) that feels overwhelming or formidable, like an army unit would be.
The Overall Sense of the Word

Whether used literally or figuratively, "battalion" always carries the feeling of scale, organization, and collective strength. A single soldier is just one person. A battalion is a force. That is the heart of what the word means.
1552:
A batten is a long, narrow, flat strip of a rigid material — almost always wood, though sometimes metal, fibreglass, or plastic. Picture a short wooden plank, then imagine it sliced lengthwise into a much thinner, narrower strip. That strip is a batten.

What makes a batten different from just "a piece of wood" is its specific shape and purpose: it is always significantly longer than it is wide, and it is relatively thin. Its job, in nearly every situation where the word is used, is to hold, stiffen, secure, or support something else.
Where You Will Encounter This Word

The word "batten" appears in several distinct areas of life. Each use is a bit different, but the underlying idea — a slim, rigid strip doing a structural or supportive job — runs through all of them.

1. In Construction and Roofing

This is probably the most common everyday use of the word.

When a house is being built, the sloping wooden framework of the roof is covered not directly with tiles, but first with a layer of thin horizontal strips of wood nailed across the roof frame. These strips are battens. The roof tiles or slates then sit on top of and hook onto these battens, row by row, like teeth on a comb.

So if you ever look at a roof being constructed before the tiles are placed, you will see a grid of wooden strips running across it — those are the battens.

The same principle is used on walls. A wall batten is a thin strip of wood fixed horizontally (or sometimes vertically) onto a brick or concrete wall, and the finishing layer — wooden cladding, plasterboard, or panelling — is then nailed or screwed onto those battens. The battens create a slight air gap and give the outer surface something solid to attach to.

2. In Carpentry: Batten Doors and Joining Boards

You may have seen old-fashioned doors in barns, sheds, or rustic cottages that look like they are made of several vertical wooden planks standing side by side. Because individual planks can warp and separate over time, shorter horizontal strips of wood are nailed across the back of those planks to hold them all together as one rigid surface. Those cross-pieces on the back are battens.

This type of door is literally called a batten door or a ledge and batten door. The battens are the reinforcing strips; they stop the door from twisting or falling apart.

More broadly, a batten can be any flat strip of wood used to strengthen or hold a surface together — to stop it from bending, buckling, or coming loose.

3. In Sailing

Here, battens serve a beautifully clever purpose.

A sail on a sailing boat is not a flat, stiff surface — it billows and curves in the wind. But if it billows too loosely, especially near the trailing edge (called the leech), it flaps and loses its aerodynamic shape. To keep the sail in the correct, efficient curved shape, sailmakers sew a series of narrow horizontal pockets into the sail fabric. Into each of these pockets, a batten is slid — a long, slender strip of fibreglass, carbon fibre, or flexible wood.

These battens hold the sail's curved shape, prevent flapping, and allow the sail to work efficiently. If you look at a sail closely, you will often notice horizontal lines across it — those are the batten pockets, with the battens inside.

A full-length batten runs all the way from one edge of the sail to the other; a partial batten only goes partway in.

4. In Theatre and Stage Lighting

Walk backstage in a theatre and look up. You will see a series of horizontal metal bars or pipes hanging above the stage at various heights, suspended from the ceiling by ropes or motorised systems. These bars can be raised and lowered. Each one of these bars is called a batten.

Lighting battens have stage lights clipped onto them. Scenery battens hold painted backdrops or flat scenery panels. Borders (fabric strips that hide the upper workings of the stage from the audience) are hung from battens too.

In this context, the batten is essentially the horizontal bar from which things are hung above the stage. It is a core piece of theatre infrastructure.

5. In Flooring

When wooden floors are laid, especially over a concrete base, battens are often used as the first step. Thin strips of treated wood (the battens) are fixed to the concrete surface, and then the actual floorboards are nailed on top of them. The battens raise the floor slightly above the cold, hard concrete, allow air circulation, and give the floorboards a surface to grip onto.

Across all of these uses, the word "batten" always refers to a long, narrow, flat, rigid strip, and it always serves a structural, supportive, or organising function. It holds tiles in place, keeps planks together, maintains a sail's shape, supports lights above a stage, and raises a wooden floor off concrete.

The word is practical and workmanlike — you will find it in the vocabulary of builders, carpenters, sailors, and theatre technicians. The moment you hear it, picture a thin strip of material doing a quiet, reliable job of holding or shaping something bigger.
1553:
"Batten down the hatches" means to prepare yourself for a difficult, dangerous, or challenging situation that is coming. It is a call to take protective action before trouble arrives — not after.

Think of it as saying: "Something tough is on the way. Get ready. Protect yourself now."
Where It Comes From (The Literal Meaning)

To truly understand this idiom, you need to picture an old sailing ship out at sea.

Hatches are the openings (like trapdoors) cut into the flat top surface of a ship — the deck. These openings allow sailors to go down into the lower levels of the ship, where the cargo, supplies, and living quarters are stored. In calm weather, these openings are left uncovered so people and goods can move in and out freely.

Battens are long, flat strips of wood or metal.

When a storm was approaching, sailors had to cover these hatch openings with thick, waterproof canvas sheets (called tarpaulins) to stop seawater from flooding into the ship. They then hammered or pressed the battens over the edges of the canvas to hold everything down tightly and securely. This whole process — securing the hatches before the storm hit — was called "battening down the hatches."

So the literal action was: close everything up and lock it down tight before the storm destroys us.
How the Meaning Jumped from Ships to Everyday Life

Over time, as people used more and more language borrowed from the world of sailing, this phrase left the sea and entered everyday conversation. The "storm" stopped meaning a real weather event and started meaning any incoming difficulty — a financial crisis, a tough challenge, bad news, an argument, or a hard period in life. The "hatches" stopped being literal openings in a ship and started meaning your resources, your defences, your plans.

The core idea stayed exactly the same: close up, protect yourself, and get ready before the trouble hits.
The Exact Feeling the Idiom Carries

This idiom carries a sense of urgency and seriousness. It is not used for small, everyday inconveniences. You wouldn't say "batten down the hatches — my coffee is cold." It is used when something significantly challenging, threatening, or turbulent is expected.

It also carries a sense of action and agency. It is not passive. It is a command, a call to do something — to prepare actively, not to simply worry or wait.

Additionally, there is a sense of anticipation built into it. The difficulty has not yet arrived — but it is coming, and you can see it on the horizon. That is the key moment when this idiom applies: the gap between knowing trouble is coming and trouble actually arriving.

Business:
"The economy is heading into a recession. Every company needs to batten down the hatches and cut unnecessary costs."

Weather (where the literal and figurative blur together):
"The forecast says a massive storm is coming this weekend. Batten down the hatches and stay indoors."

Personal life:
"Her parents are coming to visit for two weeks and they always cause drama. She's battening down the hatches."

Politics/News:
"The government is battening down the hatches ahead of the financial report, knowing the figures will be bad."

Spoken warning to a group:
"Batten down the hatches, everyone — the audit team arrives on Monday."
The Grammar: How to Use It Correctly

• The full phrase is "batten down the hatches" — all four words together.
  • It is most commonly used as a command or instruction: "Batten down the hatches!"
  • It can also be used in a describing form: "The team is battening down the hatches." (present continuous) or "The company battened down the hatches." (past tense)
  • The word "batten" here functions as a verb, meaning to fasten or secure using battens.
What Makes This Idiom Different from Similar Expressions

"Brace yourself" — similar, but more about mentally preparing for a shock or emotional blow. "Batten down the hatches" is broader and more action-oriented — it implies taking practical, real-world steps to prepare.

"Hunker down" — very close in meaning. "Hunker down" means to settle in and endure a difficult period by staying put and riding it out. The difference is subtle: "batten down the hatches" emphasises the preparation phase, while "hunker down" emphasises the enduring phase.

"Prepare for the worst" — a plain, direct expression with no imagery. "Batten down the hatches" is more vivid, more dramatic, and more colourful because it paints a picture of sailors in a storm.

"Circle the wagons" — another idiom meaning to come together defensively when under threat. But this one emphasises group unity and defence, while "batten down the hatches" focuses more on individual or organisational preparation.
A Tip to Remember It Forever

Picture this scene in your mind: a small wooden ship, the sky turning black, waves growing tall, and sailors running across the deck, hammering down covers over every opening before the storm swallows them whole.

That image is the idiom. Whenever life presents you with a storm on the horizon — a crisis, a threat, a hard stretch ahead — and you or someone else takes steps to prepare and protect, that is the moment to say: "It's time to batten down the hatches."
1554:
To batter something means to hit it hard, repeatedly, and with great force — usually to the point of causing serious damage. This is the heart of the word. It is much stronger and more violent than simply "hit" or "strike." A single blow is never battering. What makes battering distinctive is the relentless, sustained nature of the action: blow after blow after blow.

Think of someone trying to break down a locked door in an emergency. They don't knock politely. They pound it with their fists, ram it with their shoulder, kick it again and again — that is battering. The door takes repeated punishment until it gives way.
Meaning 1: To Strike a Person Repeatedly and Violently

When the object of "batter" is a human being, the word implies a brutal, one-sided, sustained physical attack. This is the word used in legal, medical, and journalistic contexts when describing serious assault, domestic violence, or abuse.

"He was arrested for battering his wife."
"The attackers battered him until he lost consciousness."
"The victim had been badly battered."

This is a weighty, serious word in this context. It is not used lightly. It implies that the person being attacked was overwhelmed, could not easily defend themselves, and suffered real harm.
Meaning 2: To Strike an Object Repeatedly

You can batter objects too — doors, walls, locks, or anything you are trying to break, force open, or destroy through repeated powerful blows.

"Firefighters battered the door down with an axe."
"He battered the old lock with a hammer until it broke."
"Protesters battered the gates of the building."

A key phrase that comes from this use is "batter down" — meaning to knock something down by battering it. You will often hear "batter down a door" or "batter down a wall."

This is one of the most common ways "batter" is used, and it feels completely natural because nature — storms, wind, waves, rain — never strikes just once. It keeps going, which is exactly the spirit of the word.

"Huge waves battered the coastline throughout the night."
"The hurricane battered the island for six hours."
"The old lighthouse had been battered by storms for decades."
"Fierce winds battered the trees, snapping several branches."

Notice that in all these cases, there is continuous, repeated force being applied against something. The sea doesn't hit the cliff once. It hits it endlessly. That is why "batter" is the perfect word here.
Meaning 4: The Figurative Use (No Physical Hitting Involved)

"Batter" is also widely used in a metaphorical sense, when something is being damaged severely — not by physical blows, but by financial loss, emotional pain, repeated setbacks, or public criticism. The idea of sustained, damaging repeated impact carries over perfectly into these non-physical situations.

"The company's share price was battered by the scandal." (The scandal hit its value again and again, causing serious damage.)

"His self-confidence was battered by years of criticism." (Repeated criticism wore his confidence down, blow by blow.)

"The team was battered by injuries all season long." (Problem after problem kept striking them down.)

"The new government's reputation was battered within its first month." (It suffered hit after hit to its image.)

In all these cases, the structure is the same: something takes repeated, damaging hits from a force it cannot easily stop.

There is one separate and much gentler use of "batter" in the kitchen. To batter food means to coat it in a thick liquid mixture — made of flour, eggs, and liquid — before frying it. This mixture is called batter (the noun), and the act of coating food in it is "to batter" it.

"She battered the fish fillets and dropped them into the hot oil."
"Battered prawns are a favourite at seaside restaurants."
"He battered the onion rings before deep-frying them."

This use has nothing to do with hitting. It simply means: dip the food into the batter mixture and coat it. The word "battered" in a food context (as in "battered cod") is extremely common in British English especially, and simply means the food has been coated and fried this way.
The Word "Battered" — The Past Form Used as a Description

Because "batter" describes sustained, damaging force, its past form — battered — is very commonly used as an adjective to describe something or someone that has clearly taken a lot of punishment over time and shows the damage.

"A battered old suitcase" — a suitcase that has been knocked around so much it looks beaten up and worn.
"A battered face" — a face showing the damage of repeated blows.
"A battered economy" — an economy that has suffered repeated hard hits.
"Battered and bruised" — a very common phrase meaning deeply damaged but still alive and going.

You will also see compound adjectives built on this pattern: storm-battered (damaged by storms), wind-battered (lashed and damaged by wind), battle-battered (worn down by fighting). These are elegant, vivid ways to describe things.
Tone and Connotation — What the Word Feels Like

"Batter" is never a neutral word. Even when used about the weather, it carries a sense of ferocity and relentlessness. It suggests that whatever is being battered is not having an easy time — it is under siege, taking hit after hit, being worn down. The word naturally creates a picture in your mind of something struggling to hold together under sustained assault.

Compare it to similar words: "hit" is neutral and describes a single action. "Beat" is stronger. "Pound" is very strong and rapid. "Batter" is in the same territory as pound — relentless, forceful, repeated — but with an even stronger sense of damage and overwhelm.
Summary of All Uses at a Glance

"Batter" in every non-cooking sense always means: repeated, forceful impact that causes damage. Whether the thing doing the battering is a pair of fists, ocean waves, a hurricane, a financial crisis, or years of criticism — the word always paints a picture of something being hit hard, over and over, until it breaks, weakens, or suffers visible harm.

In the kitchen, it means something completely separate: to coat food in a liquid flour mixture before frying.

Master those two tracks — the violent/forceful one and the culinary one — and you have complete command of this word.
1555:
Battered describes something — or someone — that has taken a lot of rough, damaging treatment and shows clear signs of it. The single most important thing to understand about this word is that the damage isn't from one quick accident. It comes from repeated blows, long exposure to harsh conditions, or sustained rough handling over time. The word always paints a picture of visible, accumulated wear or harm.

Outside of one specific cooking sense (which we'll cover), battered always feels heavy and a little sad. It is a stronger, more expressive word than simply "damaged" or "old."

1. Physically Damaged Objects

This is the most everyday use. When an object is battered, it means it has taken a lot of physical punishment — it's dented, scratched, torn, or misshapen from years of rough use or harsh treatment. It doesn't just look old; it looks like it has been through a fight.

Examples:

  • A battered old suitcase — covered in dents and scratches from years of travel
  • A battered car — the kind with dents all over its body from years of rough driving
  • A battered book — with a torn cover, bent pages, and a broken spine
  • A battered hat — squashed out of shape from being worn for decades

An important nuance: "battered" often carries a hint of a back-story. When you call something battered, you're implying it has a history — that it has lived through a lot. This is why writers sometimes use the word deliberately to add character to an object. A "battered old guitar" feels richer and more soulful than a "damaged guitar."

2. A Person Who Has Been Physically Beaten

When used to describe a person, "battered" means they have been hit or physically harmed — usually repeatedly. This is a very serious and emotionally heavy use of the word.

  • "He came home from the brawl looking completely battered." — meaning bruised, cut, and beaten up
  • A battered woman or battered wife — a woman who has been subjected to ongoing domestic violence

This sense is so strongly associated with victims of repeated physical violence that it gave rise to serious legal and psychological terms like "Battered Woman Syndrome" — a recognized condition describing the psychological effects of long-term domestic abuse on a victim.

So when you see "battered" applied to a person in a serious context, treat it with gravity. It's rarely used lightly.

3. Emotionally or Mentally Worn Down

"Battered" can also describe a person's inner emotional state — not physical injury, but the feeling of being worn down by life, stress, failure, or hardship.

  • "After months of rejection, she felt battered and hopeless."
  • "The team was battered by the string of losses." (not physically hurt, but emotionally crushed)
  • "His confidence was battered by years of harsh criticism."

Here, the logic is the same: just as a physical object gets battered from repeated blows, a person's spirit, confidence, or heart can get battered from repeated emotional hits.

4. Places or Things Beaten by Weather or Force

This is extremely common. When a storm, hurricane, waves, or any powerful natural force repeatedly strikes a place or thing, we say it was battered.

  • "The coastline was battered by the hurricane for three days."
  • "The small boat survived the battered crossing of the rough sea."
  • "A battered fishing village" — one that has endured decades of storms

The word works perfectly here because storms aren't a one-second event; they pound and lash repeatedly, and "battered" captures that repeated, relentless quality.

5. Food: Coated in Batter and Fried (Completely Different Meaning!)

This is the one meaning that has nothing to do with damage, harm, or hardship. In cooking, battered simply means food that has been coated in batter — a thick liquid mixture of flour, eggs, and milk or water — and then deep-fried.

  • Battered fish — the heart of the famous British dish "fish and chips"
  • Battered onion rings
  • Battered chicken

This meaning is entirely separate from all the others. It's named after a different word ("batter" as in the cooking mixture). So if you see "battered" in a restaurant menu or a recipe, don't worry — nothing has been hurt. It just means fried in a crispy coating!

The simplest way to tell the two apart: if "battered" comes before a food item, it's about cooking. In any other context, it carries the idea of damage or hardship.
How "Battered" Feels Compared to Similar Words

Understanding a word fully means knowing how it differs from its neighbors:

Damaged is a general, neutral word. It simply means something is not in perfect condition. It carries no emotion. A "damaged table" could have a small chip. A "battered table" has clearly been through something — it's visibly beaten up, with a story behind it.

Worn suggests gradual fading or thinning from regular use — like a worn carpet or a worn pair of shoes. It's gentle. "Battered" is not gentle. It implies harsher, more violent treatment.

Broken means something has actually come apart or stopped functioning. A broken vase is in pieces. A battered vase is dented and scarred but still whole. "Battered" describes surviving damage, not complete destruction.

Beat-up is an informal, casual version of "battered" and means essentially the same thing for objects and people. "Battered" is more formal and more emotionally weighty.
The One Feeling That Ties It All Together

Across almost every non-cooking use, "battered" carries a consistent emotional weight. It whispers: this has been through a lot. It has endured repeated punishment. It is still here — but you can see every bit of what it has been through. There's something both tough and sad in the word at the same time.

This is why writers love it. "A battered old lighthouse standing against the sea" tells you far more about that lighthouse's character than "an old lighthouse." The word does double duty — it describes physical condition and implies a whole history of endurance.

1556: The word battery has several distinct meanings depending on the context. Each meaning is used in everyday life, law, military settings, or sports. Here is a thorough look at all of them.

This is the meaning most people think of first. A battery is a device that stores chemical energy and converts it into electrical energy when needed. Inside a battery, chemicals react with each other in a way that pushes electrons through a circuit, producing electric current.

Every battery has two terminals — a positive end (+) and a negative end (−). When you connect a battery to a device (like a torch), electrons flow from the negative end, through the device, and back to the positive end. This flow of electrons is what powers the device.

Two main types:

  • Non-rechargeable batteries (also called primary batteries): These are used once and thrown away when the chemicals run out. The AA, AAA, C, D, and 9V batteries you buy in a shop are examples.
  • Rechargeable batteries (also called secondary batteries): These can be charged and discharged many times. The battery in your phone, laptop, electric car, and wireless headphones is rechargeable. Lithium-ion batteries are the most common type today.

A note on "cell" vs. "battery": Technically, a cell is a single electrochemical unit, and a battery is a collection of cells connected together. However, in everyday language, even a single AA cell is called a "battery," and that usage is perfectly accepted.

Examples of batteries in the world around you:

  • The flat rectangular battery inside a smartphone
  • The large battery pack under the floor of an electric vehicle
  • A 9-volt battery used in smoke detectors
  • A car's lead-acid battery, which starts the engine

In law, battery means the intentional and unlawful physical contact with another person without their consent. It does not require serious injury — even an unwanted touch can legally count as battery if it is done intentionally and is harmful or offensive.

For example, if someone walks up to you and slaps you, that is battery. If a doctor performs surgery on you without your consent, that could also be considered battery under the law.

You may have heard the phrase "assault and battery." These are actually two separate things:

  • Assault is threatening someone or making them fear that they are about to be physically harmed.
  • Battery is the actual physical contact that follows.

In everyday speech, people often use "assault" to mean both, but in strict legal terms, battery is specifically the physical act, not just the threat.

In military contexts, a battery is a group of artillery weapons — such as cannons, howitzers, or rocket launchers — that operate together as a unit under a single commander.

Think of it like a team. Just as soldiers in infantry are grouped into squads, platoons, and companies, artillery soldiers are grouped into batteries. A battery typically consists of several guns or launchers, the soldiers who operate them, and supporting equipment.

Example: "The artillery battery opened fire from the hilltop."

A battery in this sense is roughly equivalent to a company in size — usually around 100–200 personnel.

The word can also refer to a fixed installation of heavy guns, such as a coastal defense battery (a row of large guns built along a coastline to defend against enemy ships).
4. A Group or Series of Similar Things

Used more broadly, battery can mean a set or collection of similar things used together, especially for a common purpose. This use is borrowed from the military sense of guns lined up together.

You will often hear this in phrases like:

  • "A battery of tests" — a large set of tests given together, such as a medical battery of tests (blood test, urine test, imaging scans, etc.) or a psychological battery of assessments.
  • "A battery of questions" — a rapid, extensive series of questions asked one after another.
  • "A battery of lawyers" — a team of several lawyers working together.

The key idea is many of the same thing, all working together or applied in sequence.

In baseball, the word battery refers specifically to the pitcher and the catcher together, considered as a pair. These two players work in close coordination — the pitcher throws the ball, and the catcher signals what pitch to throw and catches it. Because they function as a unit, they are called the battery.

Example: "The starting battery for tonight's game is their ace pitcher and veteran catcher."

Although these meanings seem unrelated on the surface, they share an underlying idea of things grouped or combined to deliver force or power. Multiple artillery guns lined up together deliver firepower; multiple electrochemical cells connected together deliver electrical power; a group of tests or questions delivers a thorough examination all at once. The legal meaning follows a different path but is part of the same word's rich history in English.
